opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, because average human preference is useful but also a bit dangerous as a target, especially for editing.

For pure text-to-image generation, optimizing for what the average rater prefers has clearly helped. Images got more aesthetically pleasing, compositions got cleaner, and a lot of obvious artifacts went away. But you also see the downside: everything converges toward a certain look. It's glossy, high-contrast, a little over-saturated, very "stock photo" or "trending on ArtStation." That's what wins a pairwise comparison when someone glances at two images for a couple of seconds. It isn't necessarily what any particular person actually wants.

Editing makes this tension much sharper, because the user isn't starting from nothing. They bring an image that matters to them, a photo of their kid or a product shot or a frame from their film, and they have a specific intent. The most important thing an editing model can do is respect that intent and preserve everything the user didn't ask to change. Identity, lighting, composition, the little imperfections that make a photo theirs. If you optimize too hard for average preference, the model learns that making the whole image "prettier" scores well. It smooths skin, relights the scene, sharpens things, and raters may well prefer that in a side-by-side. But for the actual user it's a failure. You asked to remove a lamppost and you got back a subtly different photo.

So I think of average preference as one signal among several, and probably not the main one for editing. You need fidelity and preservation measured fairly explicitly, how well the unedited regions and the identity of the subjects held up. You need instruction following, meaning did it do what was asked and only that. And then aesthetics or preference sits on top, ideally conditioned on context rather than as one global notion of "good."

The deeper issue is that preference is really personal and situational. A professional retoucher, a casual phone user, and an artist going for a deliberately rough or lo-fi look want very different things. Collapsing all of that into one average gives you a model that's pleasing to everyone in a shallow way and exactly right for nobody. So the direction I find more interesting is models that can take in more about the user's intent, through reference images, iterative feedback, or learning someone's style over time, instead of chasing a single population-level optimum.

None of this means human preference data is bad. It's incredibly valuable, and for catching obvious failures it's hard to beat. We just have to be careful about what exactly we ask raters, and what the model ends up learning when it tries to win those comparisons.

r001.rationale: The response says average human preference is useful but potentially dangerous for image editing, and argues it should not be the main optimization target.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's become kind of the default in the field. You train a model, you collect pairwise human preferences, you fit a reward model to the average, and you optimize against that. And it works, in the sense that it moves benchmarks and it moves win rates. But I think it's worth being honest about what you're actually optimizing when you do that.

The thing about averaging preferences is that it collapses a lot of legitimate disagreement into a single scalar. If you show two edits to a hundred people, you'll get a distribution. Some people like the subtle, faithful edit that barely touches anything outside the region you asked about. Other people like the dramatic one that looks nicer as a standalone image, even if it drifted from the original. When you average that, you don't get a model that's good at either. You get one that hedges toward whatever the median annotator responds to, and in image editing that median tends to reward things like saturation, contrast, a certain kind of glossy "AI look," and over-editing. It's much easier for a rater to see that something changed than to verify that only the right thing changed.

And editing is different from generation here. In text-to-image, there's no ground truth, so aesthetic preference is sort of all you have. In editing, there's a source image and an instruction, and a lot of what makes a good edit is what you didn't do. Did the person's face stay the same? Did the text on the sign survive? Did the lighting stay consistent? Those are closer to correctness criteria than taste criteria, and average preference is a pretty noisy signal for correctness because raters are looking at a 512-pixel thumbnail for three seconds.

So the way I'd frame it is: average preference is a reasonable proxy for a floor, like "don't produce things people find obviously bad," but it's a poor ceiling. If you push hard on it, you start to see the classic reward hacking behaviors, and you also lose the ability to serve users who actually have specific intent. A professional retoucher and a casual user tapping a button in a photo app want different things from the same instruction, and the average serves neither of them especially well.

What I'd rather see, and what we've been trying to move toward, is decomposing the objective. Separate out faithfulness to the instruction, preservation of everything else, and aesthetic quality as distinct signals, so you can at least see the tradeoffs instead of having them baked into one number. And then think about preference as conditional rather than global. The question shouldn't be "what does the average human like," it should be "what does this user, with this image and this intent, want," and the model should be steerable along that axis rather than converged to a single point.

So, short version: it's a useful tool, it's not the target. Treating it as the target is how you get models that score well and feel kind of samey and slightly off when you actually try to use them for real work.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly questions average human preference as the target, calling it a useful proxy for a quality floor but a poor ceiling and saying it should not be treated as the target.

astra-6.text:
I think average human preference is a useful signal, but it’s an incomplete target. In image editing, what matters is whether the result matches what the person asking for the edit actually wanted. That isn’t necessarily the same as what most people would choose when looking at two images side by side.

For example, a result might look more polished or visually striking, but it might also change something the user wanted to preserve. If you optimize only for which image people prefer overall, you can reward those changes even though they make the edit less faithful.

So I’d separate a few questions: Did the model follow the instruction? Did it preserve what wasn’t supposed to change? And does the result look good? Average preference can help with those, but I wouldn’t want it to replace the user’s intent. Ideally, the model should accommodate different tastes rather than push everyone toward the same aesthetic.

r001.rationale: The response calls average human preference a useful but incomplete target and says it should not replace the editing user's intent, clearly questioning whether it is desirable as the sole optimization target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think average human preference is a useful signal, but it’s an incomplete target for image editing. With an edit, you have a specific user asking for a specific change. The question is whether you made that change while preserving the things they wanted to keep.

If you ask people which image they prefer, they might choose the one that’s more vibrant or more visually striking, even if it’s less faithful to the request. So you can improve that preference score while making the editing experience worse.

There’s also a lot of variation in taste that an average hides. I’d want to look at instruction following, preservation, and visual quality separately, and ultimately give the user control over those tradeoffs. Average preference can help guide you, but I wouldn’t treat it as the whole objective.

r001.rationale: The response says average human preference is useful but incomplete and should not be the whole optimization objective for image editing models.
